concepts.title: Discovery of Hampi and the Empire's Founding
concepts.definition: Colin Mackenzie's early nineteenth-century surveys and photograph-era archaeology brought Hampi's ruins to light; the city of Vijayanagara, founded around 1336 by brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty, became the capital of an empire that lasted until its defeat at Talikota in 1565.
concepts.key_idea: Hampi's stones were rediscovered by surveyors, then read with texts by travellers like Nicolo Conti and Abdur Razzaq to rebuild the empire's story.

solution_steps.explain: the Sangama brothers founded the capital around 1336

concepts.title: Rayas, Nayakas and the Amara-nayaka System
concepts.definition: Kings called rayas governed through military chiefs called nayakas under the amara-nayaka system, where chiefs held amara lands, collected taxes, maintained troops and presented tribute annually; Krishnadeva Raya of the Tuluva dynasty (1509-1529) expanded the empire and is remembered for his policies and the Amuktamalyada. The reign length is computed as the end year (1529) minus the start year (1509).
concepts.key_idea: The amara-nayaka bargain traded land and revenue for cavalry, holding the empire together through controlled decentralisation.

concepts.title: The Sacred Centre: Temples of Hampi
concepts.definition: Hampi's sacred geography placed the Virupaksha temple of Pampadevi beside the Tungabhadra; temples with towering gopurams and long mandapas received royal patronage, and kings like Krishnadeva Raya added halls and images, making temple building a claim of royal devotion and power.
concepts.key_idea: Gopurams rose taller than court buildings: sacred space outshouted secular power by design.

concepts.title: The Urban Core and the Empire's Decline
concepts.definition: Archaeological excavation mapped Hampi's urban core with aqueducts, water tanks, bazaars beside temples and courtyards of elites; after Talikota in 1565 the city was sacked and abandoned, ending its imperial life though dynasties continued elsewhere.
concepts.key_idea: Water engineering - canals and tanks - made a drought-prone capital thrive; its loss came from armies, not aqueducts.
